content: Hepatitis A, previously referred to as infectious hepatitis or epidemic virus, is an acute infectious disease of the liver caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV), an RNA virus. The primary mode of transmission is fecal-oral, which occurs through the ingestion of contaminated food or water or direct contact with an infected individual. Tens of millions of people worldwide are estimated to contract HAV annually. The incubation period, or the time between infection and symptom onset, ranges from two to six weeks, with an average of 28 days. In regions with poor hygiene and sanitation, such as developing countries, HAV infection is highly prevalent and typically acquired during early childhood. In these cases, over 90% of infected children remain asymptomatic, and the infection confers lifelong immunity, making it clinically insignificant for those infected early in life. Conversely, in industrialized nations like the United States and Europe, HAV infection is more commonly seen in susceptible young adults, often contracted during travel to endemic areas or through contact with infected individuals. The hepatitis A virus was first identified in 1973 and was distinguished as a separate disease from other types of hepatitis during World War II. Its true prevalence and transmission routes were only recognized later. In 1995-1996, the FDA approved inactivated hepatitis A vaccines, making the disease both common and vaccine-preventable. Hepatitis A is a liver disease caused by HAV, with peak infectivity occurring approximately two weeks before the onset of jaundice. Gross examination of the liver may reveal enlargement and erythema, while microscopic findings include lymphocyte infiltration and inflammation of the portal tracts. Hepatitis A must be differentiated from other conditions that cause fever, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, icteric sclera, and elevated liver enzymes (ALT, AST), such as other viral hepatitis types, alcoholic hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis. The incidence of hepatitis A varies by era, country, and even within cities of the same country. Historically more prevalent in children, the disease is now predominantly seen in adults. In recent years, the incidence rates have become similar across all age groups. The introduction of the HAV vaccine has narrowed historical differences in prevalence among racial and ethnic populations and eliminated geographic disparities in developed countries. In developing nations with poor sanitation, up to 90% of children are infected with HAV before the age of 10. Individuals at increased risk of HAV infection include those who are not immunized and travel to endemic areas with poor sanitation and unsafe water. Additional risk factors include intravenous drug use, living with an infected person, having a sexual partner with acute HAV infection, and attending childcare centers. Screening for hepatitis A involves detecting HAV antibodies in the blood. Anti-HAV IgG remains elevated after acute disease and provides lifelong immunity. HAV infection typically results in a self-limited disease with an incubation period of approximately 28 days. While children often experience asymptomatic or unrecognized infections, over 80% of adults exhibit symptoms of acute viral hepatitis, such as fatigue, malaise, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Complications may include dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, bleeding, and, rarely, fulminant hepatitis. Prognosis depends on the patient’s age and underlying liver condition. Approximately 10-15% of patients experience a relapse of symptoms within six months of acute illness. Hepatitis A infection can present with fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Physical examination findings may include fever, jaundice, icteric sclera, abdominal tenderness, and hepatomegaly. Other findings may include rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, abdominal distension, ascites, and altered mental status. Laboratory tests are essential for diagnosing hepatitis A, as clinical and epidemiologic features alone cannot differentiate it from other types of viral hepatitis. Elevated IgM anti-HAV during the acute phase is the gold standard for diagnosis, while IgG anti-HAV remains elevated for life. Additional findings may include HAV RNA detection, elevated direct bilirubin, and elevated liver enzymes. Liver biopsy is rarely used and is reserved for unclear diagnoses or suspected relapses. Imaging studies, such as CT scans, are not typically indicated for diagnosing hepatitis A but may be performed to exclude alternative diagnoses. Abdominal ultrasound may be used to rule out other causes of hepatomegaly or chronic liver disease. Common ultrasound findings in acute hepatitis A include increased brightness of the portal vein walls and decreased liver echogenicity. There is no specific treatment for hepatitis A. Recovery from symptoms may take weeks to months. Management focuses on maintaining comfort and adequate nutritional balance, including fluid replacement for losses due to vomiting and diarrhea. Patients with fulminant hepatitis may require aggressive supportive therapy and transfer to a center capable of performing liver transplantation. Primary prevention of HAV infection includes the hepatitis A vaccine and immune globulin (IG) for intramuscular administration. The vaccine is administered in a two-dose series at 0 and 6-12 months, inducing protective antibody levels in nearly all adults. By one month after the first dose, 94-100% of adults develop protective antibody levels, with 100% achieving protection after the second dose. IG, a sterile solution of concentrated immunoglobulins, is over 85% effective in preventing HAV infection when administered intramuscularly before or within two weeks of exposure. Secondary prevention strategies have evolved to include the hepatitis A vaccine for post-exposure prophylaxis in healthy individuals aged 1-40 years. Decisions to use the vaccine or immune globulin should consider patient characteristics associated with severe manifestations of hepatitis A, such as older age and chronic liver disease.
